citation: Gunawardena, Charlotte N., & Frank J. Zittle. (1997). Social presence as a predictor of satisfaction within a computer-mediated conferencing environment. American Journal of Distance Education, 11(3), 8–26. https://doi.org/10.1080/08923649709526970
thesis: Social presence — the degree to which a communicator is perceived as a 'real person' in mediated interaction — is empirically measurable as a strong predictor of learner satisfaction even within a low-bandwidth, text-only CMC medium, provided the construct is operationalized with an instrument (the Gunawardena Social Presence Scale) built for group-based CMC rather than borrowed from face-to-face or broadcast-media research; a stepwise regression on the Fall 1993 GlobalEd inter-university computer conference (N=50) converges on a three-predictor model (social presence, perceived equal-participation opportunity, technical skill) explaining roughly 71% of variance in satisfaction, with social presence alone contributing about 60 percentage points.

sections.title: Introduction — CMC from a socio-psychological perspective
sections.summary: Situates CMC research within a socio-psychological perspective (Jones 1995; Spears & Lea 1992; Walther 1992); adopts Spears & Lea's (1992) taxonomy of three 'social cues perspective' frameworks — Short, Williams & Christie's (1976) social presence model, Rutter's (1987) cuelessness model, Kiesler, Siegel & McGuire's (1984) reduced social cues approach — and selects social presence as the most influential, the framework this study operationalizes.

sections.title: Definition of Social Presence
sections.summary: Presents Short, Williams & Christie's (1976) definition — 'the degree of salience of the other person in the interaction and the consequent salience of the interpersonal relationships' (original p.65) — as a property of the medium's capacity to transmit facial expression, gaze, posture, and nonverbal cues; links it to Argyle & Dean's (1965) 'intimacy' and Wiener & Mehrabian's (1968) 'immediacy'; positions text-based CMC as low on both relative to audio/video media.

sections.title: Research on Social Presence
sections.summary: Reviews face-to-face/ITV findings linking teacher 'immediacy' to affective learning (Kearney, Plax & Wendt-Wasco 1985; Christophel 1990; Gorham 1988) and, per Hackman & Walker (1990), to satisfaction/learning in a distance ITV class. Surveys CMC-specific findings (Walther 1992; Baym 1995) reporting positive relational behavior and 'online community' formation despite reduced cues, and compensatory emoticon use (Hiltz 1994; Walther 1992). Introduces Rafaeli's (1988, 1990) distinction between social presence (subjective) and interactivity (an actualized quality of a communication sequence).

sections.title: The Need for and Purpose of the Study
sections.summary: Identifies the gap: prior work tested teacher immediacy's effect on satisfaction/learning in ITV and face-to-face classrooms, but none had measured social presence's effect on learner satisfaction specifically within CMC, nor developed a CMC-context social-presence scale. Argues social presence should be measured from a group perspective because CMC decenters the teacher into a facilitator role. States the purpose: test social presence as a predictor of satisfaction in the Fall 1993 GlobalEd inter-university computer conference (~90 participants), plus an ancillary interest in emoticon use as an interaction effect.

sections.title: Method — participants, procedure, instrumentation
sections.summary: N=50 graduate students across five universities (San Diego State n=8, Texas A&M n=11, New Mexico n=14, Wisconsin-Madison n=7, Wyoming n=10; ~90 total across the full six-to-eight-university GlobalEd conference); 62% female, mean age 40, ~88% Caucasian. Fall 1993 semester-long text-based computer conference. Participants completed a 61-item post-conference GlobalEd Questionnaire; 52 five-point Likert items used across nine subscales/single items (Spres [social presence, 14 items, α=.88], Active, Attitude [2 items, α=.74], Barriers [2 items, α=.72], Capable, Equal, Trained, Tech [3 items, α=.83], Sat [satisfaction, 10 items, α=.87]), plus six of seventeen bi-polar items retained as a convergent-validity check on the Social Presence scale.

sections.title: Results
sections.summary: SPRES correlated strongly and positively with six bi-polar 'intimacy' indicators (r=.52-.87, p<.001), the strongest being Personal/Impersonal (r=.87), supporting SPRES's validity against Short/Williams/Christie's original conception. An initial eight-predictor stepwise regression converged on a four-predictor model (Spres, Equal, Tech, Attitude; R=.87, R²>.75, F(4,26)=19.82, p<.001) flagged as compromised by response-dropout sample shrinkage; re-running restricted to the three strongest predictors yields the reported final model (Table 4): Spres, Equal, Tech jointly explain 70.8% of variance in Sat (R=.841, R²=.708, F(3,30)=24.22, p<.001) — Spres alone ~60 points, Equal ~7, Tech ~4; no outliers, acceptable collinearity. A nonsignificant negative Equal-Sat correlation (r=-.20) is explored via scatterplot: at low social presence, low-Equal respondents rate satisfaction higher than high-Equal respondents, a difference that disappears at higher presence. Emoticon use shows no satisfaction effect at low social presence but an increasingly positive one as social presence rises ('rich-get-richer', citing Steinfield 1986).

sections.title: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.summary: Concludes social presence is a strong predictor of satisfaction even in a text-based (low-bandwidth) medium, extending Hackman & Walker's (1990) ITV finding to CMC and supporting Walther's (1992) and Baym's (1995) relational view of CMC. Per Walther's (1992) social-information-processing perspective, GlobalEd participants agreed later-conference messages were more social/personal than earlier ones (Mean 4.15/5), suggesting CMC's depersonalizing reputation may be limited to initial interactions. States practical implications: design CMC conferences to deliberately cultivate social presence, citing Johansen, Vallee & Spangler's (1988) claim that presence 'can be cultured'; cites Eastmond (1993) that interactivity/collaboration/reflectivity depend on design and moderator role, not the medium alone. Calls for future research on cognitive (not just affective) learning outcomes, individual/cultural differences, and cross-national replication.

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: central, namesake construct; origin of the 14-item Gunawardena Social Presence Scale (SPRES), a CMC-context alternative to Short, Williams & Christie's (1976) bi-polar/semantic-differential approach, convergent-validity-confirmed against it (r=.52-.87)

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: adjacent-match only, not exact — this paper's actual criterion variable is 'satisfaction' (10-item Sat scale), which bundles perceived learning, continuation-motivation, and overall valuation, not enjoyment specifically; flagged, not resolved (P/anticipatory-application)

constructs.label: self-efficacy
constructs.treatment: single-item 'Capable' subscale (confidence mastering CMC); measured but does not survive into the final three-predictor model

constructs.label: agency / interactivity
constructs.treatment: single-item 'Equal' subscale (perceived equal participation opportunity) enters the final model (~7% variance) plus a nonsignificant Equal-Sat interaction explored via scatterplot; also treated theoretically via Rafaeli's (1988, 1990) social-presence/interactivity distinction, cited but not itself operationalized as a separate scale here

conditionsNote: Strand F unit — the §3 media-condition axis (IVR/HMD, desktop-3D, 2D video, screen-based sim, conventional-instruction control, home-vs-classroom, etc.) was built for the media-comparison and simulation-learning literatures of Strands C/D and does not fit a single-medium correlational CMC study; there is no media contrast in this design (no group used a different modality). Per plan scope, Strand F units are not required to populate this axis, so it is deliberately left empty rather than force-fit. The study's actual design parameters (N=50 across 5 universities, ~90-participant GlobalEd conference, text-based asynchronous CMC, stepwise-regression correlational analysis, 52 Likert items across 9 subscales) are described in full in the .md §4 instead.

readings.claim: Social presence is empirically measurable as a strong predictor of learner satisfaction even within a low-bandwidth, text-only CMC medium.

Short, Williams & Christie's (1976) social presence — 'the degree of salience of the other person in the interaction and the consequent salience of the interpersonal relationships' — is retained as the theoretical anchor but relocated operationally: from bi-polar ratings of medium properties to Likert self-report of group experience.

The final three-predictor stepwise regression model (Spres, Equal, Tech) explains 70.8% of variance in satisfaction (R=.841, R²=.708, F(3,30)=24.22, p<.001); social presence alone contributes approximately 60 percentage points.
The paper's own abstract rounds the final model's explained variance to 'about 68%,' which does not match the R²=.708 reported in Table 4 for the same three-predictor model.

readings.claim: Emoticon use shows no satisfaction effect at low social presence but an increasingly positive effect as social presence rises — a compensatory 'rich-get-richer' pattern.

CMC's depersonalizing reputation may be limited to initial interactions rather than a fixed medium property, per Walther's (1992) social-information-processing perspective; GlobalEd participants rated later-conference messages as more social/personal.
Academic CMC conferences should be deliberately designed to cultivate social presence, since presence 'can be cultured' rather than fixed by medium bandwidth alone.

interlocutors.name: Short, John, Ederyn Williams & Bruce Christie (1976)
interlocutors.role: origin theory: the social presence model this paper operationalizes with a new CMC-context scale. Gunawardena & Zittle do not contest Short/Williams/Christie's core definition of social presence; they relocate its site of measurement from the medium's inherent bandwidth properties to participants' self-reported group experience, retaining the original bi-polar/semantic-differential items only as a convergent-validity check on the new SPRES scale rather than as the primary instrument.

interlocutors.name: Rutter, D.R. (1987)
interlocutors.role: cuelessness model, named as a competing 'social cues perspective' framework, not adopted here

interlocutors.name: Kiesler, Sara, Jane Siegel & Timothy W. McGuire (1984)
interlocutors.role: reduced social cues approach, likewise named but not adopted

interlocutors.name: Walther, Joseph B. (1992)
interlocutors.role: social information-processing perspective; cited on CMC relational development over time and on incomplete-measurement critiques of 'CMC as impersonal' claims

interlocutors.name: Rafaeli, Sheizaf (1988, 1990)
interlocutors.role: distinguishes social presence (subjective) from interactivity (actualized quality of a communication sequence)

interlocutors.name: Hackman, Michael Z. & Kathleen B. Walker (1990)
interlocutors.role: prior finding that teacher immediacy predicts satisfaction/learning in interactive television; the closest existing precedent this study extends to CMC

interlocutors.name: Gunawardena, Charlotte N. (1995)
interlocutors.role: the lead author's own earlier social-presence-theory literature review, cited as background

interlocutors.name: Spears, Russell & Martin Lea (1992)
interlocutors.role: taxonomy of social-psychological CMC approaches this paper adopts

interlocutors.name: Baym, Nancy K. (1995)
interlocutors.role: reports positive relational behavior and 'online community' formation in CMC despite reduced cues

interlocutors.name: Steinfield, Charles W. (1986)
interlocutors.role: supports the 'rich-get-richer' emoticon finding via study of social/task-oriented e-mail use

interlocutors.name: Eastmond, D.V. (1993)
interlocutors.role: argues interactivity/collaboration/reflectivity are not inherent to the medium but result from design, moderator role, and participation patterns

interlocutors.name: Johansen, R., J. Vallee & K. Spangler (1988)
interlocutors.role: claim that social presence 'can be cultured' among teleconferencing participants, supporting this paper's design-recommendation conclusion

tensions.axis: presence as technology/bandwidth-determined vs. presence as context/design-determined
tensions.note: The paper opens within Short/Williams/Christie's medium-property framing but its own findings (Walther's SIP perspective; Eastmond's design-dependent view; the 'presence can be cultured' conclusion) pull toward a context/design-determined reading — an internal drift the paper does not fully reconcile, and a direct instance of this cluster's debate axis #3 (presence as technology-determined vs. presence as psychologically/individually determined).

tensions.axis: final-model reported variance: Table 4 (70.8%) vs. abstract ('about 68%')
tensions.note: Internal inconsistency in the source text itself between the abstract's rounded summary and the body's own Table 4 statistics for the same three-predictor model; not resolved here.

tensions.axis: Equal (perceived equal-participation opportunity) as predictor vs. its own nonsignificant negative bivariate correlation with satisfaction
tensions.note: Equal enters the final regression model with a positive contribution (~7% variance) yet correlates negatively (r=-.20, ns) with satisfaction on its own; the authors flag this as a possible interaction effect with social presence rather than resolving it.

bridgeNote: vle-01's F7 finding ('Presence & the WE': 4.3 vs. 1.2 per-100 presence-coded language gap between app-users and video-only respondents; optative remarks like 'seemed isolating' and 'watch with others') is thematically adjacent to what SPRES measures, but the VLE instrument has no dedicated, validated social-presence/co-presence scale of its own — Q7/Q8 are a forced-choice able-to-use/immersion item, and F7's evidence is open-text coding of unprompted remarks, not scale responses. This unit therefore identifies a genuine instrumentation gap in the VLE rather than confirming a match to it; vle-03's 'watch with others'/'seemed isolating' exemplar quotes should be read as suggestive, not confirmatory, of an SPRES-type effect (P/anticipatory-application).
hubNote: Foundational source: origin of the Gunawardena Social Presence Scale, offered as a CMC-context alternative to Short/Williams/Christie's (1976) original semantic-differential presence measure. Confirmed cited by ped-sec-26 (Garrison, Anderson & Archer 1999, already built), which cites 'Gunawardena & Zittle (1997) on emoticon use' directly in its Social Presence section and lists Gunawardena among its pre-1999 interlocutors. Expected to also be cited by later Strand-F units still pending build at the time of this writing (plausibly Tu 2002/ped-sec-27, Biocca et al. 2003/ped-sec-29) given their shared CMC/online-learning social-presence lineage — flagged for the Phase 3 citation-network wave as a probable intra-cluster hub node alongside ped-sec-26.
